unmatched_peer.body: If the pending task (e.g. `run_get_response`) raises an exception other than `CancelledError` after being cancelled, that exception is silently swallowed here. The `await pending` after `pending.cancel()` will re-raise whatever the task raised — if the view raised a non-`CancelledError` exception (e.g. an unhandled `ValueError` in the view), it will be lost. Only `CancelledError` is caught, so other exceptions propagate up, but if the task suppressed `CancelledError` and returned normally, the result is also discarded. More critically, if `listen_for_disconnect` is the pending task and it raises `AssertionError` (the invalid message case), that `AssertionError` is swallowed here because `pending.cancel()` races with the task completing.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The `pending.cancel()` call sends a cancellation, but if the task has already completed (e.g. `listen_for_disconnect` already raised `AssertionError` before cancellation), `await pending` will re-raise `AssertionError`, which is not caught in this block. However, if `run_get_response` is the pending task and it raises something unexpected, that exception is lost. The `except asyncio.CancelledError: pass` is too broad a suppression for a general-purpose handler.

unmatched_peer.body: `done.result()` is called assuming `done` is the task that completed first. But if `listen_for_disconnect` completes first (raising `RequestAborted`), `done` is that task and `pending` is `run_get_response`. The `except RequestAborted` branch correctly handles this. However, if `run_get_response` completes first and returns a response, `done` is that task — but `listen_for_disconnect` (the pending task) may have already raised `AssertionError` before being cancelled. In that case `await pending` on line 191 re-raises `AssertionError`, which is caught by `except AssertionError` on line 200 and `body_file.close()` is called and re-raised — but the response is never sent. This is arguably correct behaviour, but the `AssertionError` catch on line 200 is only needed for the case where `listen_for_disconnect` is the `done` task, not the `pending` task. The two `try` blocks conflate different error sources.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The `done` variable can be either `run_get_response` or `listen_for_disconnect` depending on which finishes first. The `AssertionError` from `listen_for_disconnect` (invalid ASGI message) can surface from either `await pending` (line 191) or `done.result()` (line 196), but only the latter is caught. This asymmetry means an `AssertionError` from the pending task propagates uncaught past the `body_file.close()` call, leaking the file handle.

unmatched_peer.body: `body_file.close()` is called in the `except RequestAborted` and `except AssertionError` branches, but not in the normal success path after `send_response`. If `send_response` raises an exception, `body_file` is never closed. The existing code before this PR had the same pattern, but the refactor into `run_get_response` makes it more fragile. Consider wrapping the whole block in a `try/finally` to ensure `body_file.close()` is always called.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The `body_file` is a `SpooledTemporaryFile` created in `read_body`. It is closed in error branches but not guaranteed to be closed if `send_response` raises. A `try/finally` around the task block would be more robust.

unmatched_peer.body: The test uses `await asyncio.sleep(0.1)` to "let the view actually start" before sending the disconnect. This is a timing-dependent approach that could be flaky on slow CI machines. The view sleeps for `0.2` seconds, so a 0.1s delay should be sufficient in most cases, but this is a fragile pattern. A more robust approach would use an `asyncio.Event` to signal when the view has actually started executing.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The view at line 361 does `await asyncio.sleep(0.2)`, and the test waits 0.1s before sending disconnect. On a heavily loaded system, the 0.1s sleep in the test might not be enough for the view task to actually start and reach its own sleep. This is a common source of intermittent test failures.

unmatched_peer.body: `hello_with_delay` uses `time.sleep(1)` (a blocking synchronous sleep) inside what will be run as an ASGI view. This blocks the entire event loop thread for 1 second during `test_delayed_disconnect_with_body`. While it works for testing purposes (since it's a sync view run via `sync_to_async`), it makes the test suite slow. The `test_delayed_disconnect_with_body` test sends a disconnect immediately after the request, so the 1-second delay is never actually waited out — but if the disconnect handling races, the test could take up to 1 second.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The `hello_with_delay` view uses `time.sleep(1)` which is a blocking call. In the ASGI context this runs via `sync_to_async`, so it won't block the event loop, but it does mean the test could take up to 1 second if the disconnect isn't processed quickly. A shorter delay (e.g. 0.1s) would make the test faster without losing coverage.

More importantly, the example doesn't demonstrate any actual cleanup work in the `except` block — the comment says "Handle disconnect" but the only code is `raise`. A more illustrative example showing actual cleanup (e.g. closing a resource, logging) would be more useful to readers.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The purpose of this feature is to allow cleanup on disconnect. The example only shows catching and re-raising, which is the same as not catching at all. Users need to see what useful cleanup looks like in the except block.

unmatched_peer.body:
When `process_request` is done and `listen_for_disconnect` is still pending, the code calls `task.result()` on `process_request` but silently swallows any non-`AssertionError` exception it raised (e.g. an unhandled exception from the view or `send_response`). Only `RequestAborted` and `AssertionError` are handled; any other exception is caught by neither branch and is silently dropped.

In the old code, `done.result()` was called and exceptions propagated. Here, iterating over `tasks` and calling `task.result()` without a bare `raise` for unexpected exceptions means view errors are silently swallowed.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The `try/except` block only catches `RequestAborted` and `AssertionError`. Any other exception raised inside `process_request` (e.g. a programming error in the view, or an error in `send_response`) will be silently ignored because `task.result()` re-raises the stored exception, but neither `except` clause matches it, and there is no bare `except` or `raise` to propagate it. The old code did not have this problem because it called `done.result()` outside a try/except that swallowed unknown exceptions.

unmatched_peer.body: When a task is cancelled and re-raises `CancelledError`, the `except asyncio.CancelledError` branch silently swallows it. But if the task raises a *different* exception after being cancelled (e.g. the view catches `CancelledError` and raises something else), that exception is also silently dropped. There is no re-raise or propagation for unexpected exceptions from the `await task` path.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The `try/except asyncio.CancelledError` around `await task` only catches `CancelledError`. If the task raises any other exception (e.g. the view catches `CancelledError` and raises a `ValueError`), it will propagate out of the loop unhandled — but more subtly, if the task raises nothing and returns normally (because it finished between the `task.done()` check and `task.cancel()`), the cancel is a no-op and the result is never inspected. This is a minor race but worth noting.

unmatched_peer.body: `body_file.close()` is called inside the `AssertionError` handler for the `listen_for_disconnect` task, but if `process_request` raises an `AssertionError` (second iteration of the loop), `body_file.close()` is also called — and then `body_file.close()` is called again at line 224 unconditionally. This double-close is harmless for `SpooledTemporaryFile` but is inconsistent. More importantly, if an unexpected exception escapes the loop (see above), `body_file.close()` at line 224 is never reached, causing a resource leak.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The `body_file.close()` at line 224 is only reached if the loop completes without an unhandled exception. If an unexpected exception propagates out of `task.result()`, the file is never closed. A `try/finally` wrapping the task loop would be safer.

unmatched_peer.body: The documentation says Django will cancel the coroutine "if the client disconnects during a streaming response", but this only applies to ASGI. WSGI streaming responses are unaffected. The docs should clarify this is ASGI-only behavior to avoid confusion.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The feature is implemented in `ASGIHandler.handle()` and is specific to ASGI. The surrounding section does not mention ASGI, so a reader using WSGI might incorrectly expect the same behavior.

unmatched_peer.body: In `test_streaming`, after fetching the two body chunks, the test fetches one more output and then asserts a `TimeoutError` on the next. It's unclear what the third `receive_output` call at line 503 is expected to return — the comment says "Fetch the rest of the response so that coroutines are cleaned up", but there's no assertion on its content. If the streaming response only yields two chunks (`first\n` and `last\n`), what is the third message? This should be documented or asserted.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The `streaming_inner` generator yields exactly two chunks. A streaming HTTP response in ASGI typically sends `http.response.start`, then one or more `http.response.body` messages, with the last one having `more_body=False`. The third `receive_output` at line 503 likely fetches the final `http.response.body` with `more_body=False` and an empty body, but this is not asserted, making the test's intent unclear.

The annotation should be `Any` (matching the actual signature used in pydantic's protocol) to avoid misleading readers.

peer.body: The sub-bullet "Functions may be decorated if wrapped properly, i.e. using `functools.wraps`" is slightly misleading. `functools.wraps` is needed for *arbitrary* decorators to work, but `functools.cache` and `functools.lru_cache` work because they are *explicitly* registered — not because they use `functools.wraps`. The phrasing implies that any decorator using `functools.wraps` is supported, which is true, but the relationship between the two sub-bullets could be clearer to avoid confusion.
peer.rationale: The PR adds explicit support for `functools._lru_cache_wrapper` in the serializer registry. The `functools.wraps` path works via `__wrapped__` attribute propagation in `FunctionTypeSerializer`. Grouping these two mechanisms under the same parent bullet without distinguishing them may confuse readers into thinking `functools.wraps` is required for `cache`/`lru_cache` support.

unmatched_peer.body: `functools._lru_cache_wrapper` is a private/internal CPython implementation detail. Relying on it may break across Python versions or alternative Python implementations (e.g., PyPy). A more robust approach would be to obtain the type dynamically, e.g. `type(functools.lru_cache(lambda: None))`, or to check `hasattr(value, '__wrapped__')` combined with `isinstance` checks in the serializer logic.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The leading underscore in `functools._lru_cache_wrapper` signals it is not part of the public API. While it has been stable in CPython for a long time, it is not guaranteed to remain so, and it is not available in all Python implementations. The public API does not expose this type directly.

unmatched_peer.body: The test `test_serialize_decorated_functions` only calls `assertSerializedEqual`, which checks that the serialized output round-trips. It does not verify the actual serialized string (e.g., that `function_with_lru_cache` serializes to `'tests.migrations.test_writer.function_with_lru_cache'`). A test using `assertSerializedResultEqual` would make the expected output explicit and catch regressions in the serialized form.
unmatched_peer.rationale: Other tests in the same class (e.g., `test_serialize_functions`) use both `assertSerializedEqual` and `assertSerializedResultEqual` to pin the exact output. Without pinning the string, a change that produces a wrong but round-trippable result (e.g., serializing to the wrapper's internal name) would go undetected.

unmatched_peer.body: When `error_messages is None`, `self.error_messages` is assigned the class-level `default_error_messages` dict directly (not a copy). This means any mutation of `self.error_messages` on an instance would silently mutate the shared class attribute, affecting all future instances. The `error_messages is not None` branch correctly creates a new dict via `|`, but the `None` branch should also produce a copy.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The `else` branch (`self.default_error_messages | error_messages`) creates a new dict, but the `if` branch returns the same object as `self.default_error_messages`. If any code ever does `paginator.error_messages['invalid_page'] = '...'`, it would corrupt the class-level default for all subsequent instances.
unmatched_peer.suggestion:
self.error_messages = (
            self.default_error_messages.copy()
            if error_messages is None
            else self.default_error_messages | error_messages
        )

unmatched_peer.body: `error_messages` is documented as a `.. attribute::` but it is actually a constructor parameter (like `orphans` and `allow_empty_first_page`, which are documented as `.. attribute::` too — so this follows the existing convention). However, the section header says "The `error_messages` argument lets you override…" which is accurate, but the attribute name in the class signature at line 17 is `error_messages=None`. The `default_error_messages` class attribute (which users may want to override in a subclass) is not documented at all, even though it is the primary extension point for subclasses.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The PR introduces `default_error_messages` as a class attribute intended for subclass customization (following the Django forms pattern cited in the PR discussion), but the docs only describe the constructor argument. Subclassers have no documented way to know they can override `default_error_messages`.

unmatched_peer.body: The test does not cover the case where an unknown/extra key is passed in `error_messages` (e.g. a typo like `{'invlaid_page': '...'}`) — the dict merge would silently ignore it and the default message would still be used. A test asserting that only known keys are accepted (or at least documenting the silent-ignore behaviour) would help catch user mistakes.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The current implementation uses `self.default_error_messages | error_messages`, which silently accepts any keys. There is no validation that the provided keys are among the known set (`invalid_page`, `min_page`, `no_results`). This is a usability concern worth at least a test that documents the behaviour.

unmatched_peer.body:
The `is_root_model` check uses `in` on `base.fullname`, which is a substring match. For example, a class whose full name happens to contain the string `'pydantic.root_model.RootModel'` as a substring (e.g. `'some.module.pydantic.root_model.RootModel_extended'`) would incorrectly be treated as a `RootModel` subclass. Use an equality check instead:
```python
is_root_model = any(base.fullname == ROOT_MODEL_FULLNAME for base in info.mro[:-1])
```
This matches the pattern used for `is_settings` on line 444.
unmatched_peer.rationale: The `is_settings` check on line 444 uses `== BASESETTINGS_FULLNAME` (equality), while this new check uses `ROOT_MODEL_FULLNAME in base.fullname` (substring). The substring approach is fragile and inconsistent with the established pattern in this file.
unmatched_peer.suggestion: is_root_model = any(base.fullname == ROOT_MODEL_FULLNAME for base in info.mro[:-1])

unmatched_peer.body:
`args[0]` is accessed without checking whether `args` is non-empty. If a `RootModel` subclass has no fields (e.g. `class Pets1(RootModel[List[str]]): pass`), `args` will be empty and this will raise an `IndexError` at analysis time, crashing the mypy plugin.

A guard is needed:
```python
if is_root_model and args:
    args[0].kind = ARG_POS if args[0].kind == ARG_NAMED else ARG_OPT
```
unmatched_peer.rationale: The `get_field_arguments` call returns arguments based on `fields`. For `Pets1` in the test module (which has `pass` and inherits `root` from the generic base), the inherited `root` field may or may not be present in `args` depending on how `collect_fields` resolves it. If `args` is empty, `args[0]` will raise `IndexError`.

unmatched_peer.body: `error_extra_fields_on_root_model` declares its `api` parameter as `CheckerPluginInterface`, but it is called from `collect_fields` where `self._api` is a `SemanticAnalyzerPluginInterface`. These are different interfaces — `CheckerPluginInterface` is used during type-checking, while `SemanticAnalyzerPluginInterface` is used during semantic analysis. The type annotation should be `SemanticAnalyzerPluginInterface` to match the actual call site.
unmatched_peer.rationale: In `collect_fields` (line 609), the call is `error_extra_fields_on_root_model(self._api, stmt)`. `self._api` is typed as `SemanticAnalyzerPluginInterface` (set in `__init__`). Compare with `error_untyped_fields` which correctly uses `SemanticAnalyzerPluginInterface`. The other error functions using `CheckerPluginInterface` (e.g. `error_from_attributes`, `error_default_and_default_factory_specified`) are called from checker callbacks, not semantic analysis callbacks.
